description: The law of supply, why supply curves slope up, and the factors that shift supply versus a movement along it.
content_html:
What Is Supply?

Supply is the amount of a good or service that producers are willing and able to sell at each possible price. Notice those two words: “willing” means producers want to sell, and “able” means they can actually produce and deliver it. A farmer who wants to sell 1,000 tonnes of wheat but can only harvest 200 tonnes is “able” to supply just 200 tonnes, regardless of willingness.

Supply is always measured over a specific time period — for example, the number of loaves a bakery can supply per week, or the number of cars a manufacturer can produce per month. Supply and price are closely linked: in most markets, the higher the price, the more producers want to supply.

The Law of Supply

The law of supply states that there is a positive relationship between price and quantity supplied, all other things being equal. Think about a coffee shop: if the price of a cup of coffee rises from £3 to £4.50, the owner has a stronger incentive to brew and sell more cups — the higher price covers costs more easily and leaves a larger profit on every sale. Conversely, if the price falls, it may no longer be worth producing as much, so the quantity supplied contracts.

The phrase “all other things being equal” (often written as the Latin ceteris paribus) is vital. It means we are changing only the price and holding everything else — technology, input costs, taxes — constant. In the real world, several things change at once, which is why we study each factor separately.

Key Fact

The law of supply: as price rises, quantity supplied rises; as price falls, quantity supplied falls — ceteris paribus. This gives the supply curve its upward slope.

The Supply Curve

Economists draw a supply curve on a graph with price on the vertical axis (P) and quantity supplied on the horizontal axis (Q). Because of the law of supply, this curve slopes upward from left to right. At a low price, producers supply a small quantity; at a high price, they supply a large quantity. Each point on the curve represents one price–quantity combination.

For example, a clothing manufacturer might supply 5,000 jackets per week when each jacket sells for £40, but 9,000 jackets per week when the price rises to £70. If you plotted these pairs on a graph, the curve connecting them would rise as you move to the right — higher price, higher quantity supplied.

This is one of the most common sources of confusion in GCSE Economics. A movement along the supply curve happens when only the price of the good changes. If the price rises, producers move up the existing curve, supplying more — this is called an extension of supply. If the price falls, they move down the existing curve, supplying less — a contraction of supply.

A shift in the supply curve happens when something other than the price of the good changes — for example, production costs fall, or new technology is introduced. This shifts the entire curve: a shift to the RIGHT means more is supplied at every price (an increase in supply); a shift to the LEFT means less is supplied at every price (a decrease in supply).

The key test: if the change is caused by a price change, it’s a movement. If it’s caused by anything else, it’s a shift.

Factors That Shift the Supply Curve

Several non-price factors can shift the supply curve to the left or right. The most important are costs of production, technology, taxes, subsidies, weather or natural factors, the number of firms in the market, and the productivity of factors of production.

1. Costs of Production

Costs of production are the expenses firms face when making their product. If costs rise — for instance, if the price of steel rises for a car manufacturer, or if energy bills double for a bakery — it becomes more expensive to produce each unit. Firms respond by supplying less at every price, so the supply curve shifts LEFT. Conversely, if costs fall (perhaps because wages fall or cheaper raw materials become available), firms can profitably supply more, shifting the curve RIGHT.

2. Technology

Improvements in technology allow firms to produce the same output with fewer inputs, lowering the cost per unit. A car manufacturer that introduces robotic assembly lines can produce more vehicles per day than a fully manual production line — reducing unit costs and increasing supply at every price. Technological improvements typically shift the supply curve to the RIGHT.

Key Fact

Supply shifts RIGHT (increases) when: costs fall, technology improves, a subsidy is granted, more firms enter the market, productivity rises, or (for agricultural goods) weather is favourable. Supply shifts LEFT (decreases) when: costs rise, a tax is imposed, firms leave the market, or bad weather destroys a harvest.

3. Taxes and Subsidies

Government intervention directly affects supply. An indirect tax on production (such as an environmental levy on a factory’s carbon emissions) adds to the firm’s costs, making production more expensive and shifting supply LEFT. A subsidy, on the other hand, is a financial payment from the government that reduces production costs. For example, a government subsidy for solar panel manufacturers lowers their costs, allowing them to supply more panels at every price, shifting supply RIGHT.

4. Weather and Natural Factors

For primary-sector goods — particularly agricultural products like wheat, coffee, and cocoa — weather has a major influence on supply. A warm, dry summer and plentiful rainfall can produce a bumper harvest, shifting the supply curve RIGHT and driving prices down. A frost, drought, or disease (such as a coffee leaf-rust outbreak) destroys crops, shifting supply LEFT and pushing prices up. This is why food prices can be volatile from year to year.

5. Number of Firms and Productivity

Two further non-price factors shift the supply curve. First, the number of firms in a market: if new producers enter, total market supply increases and the supply curve shifts RIGHT. If firms exit — for example, because the market becomes unprofitable — market supply falls and the curve shifts LEFT. Second, productivity: if workers or machines become more efficient, each unit of output requires fewer inputs, lowering unit costs. Higher productivity therefore shifts the supply curve to the RIGHT, just as a fall in input costs does.

An extension of supply occurs when the price of the good rises and producers supply a greater quantity as a result — this is a movement UP the supply curve. A contraction of supply occurs when the price of the good falls and producers supply a smaller quantity — a movement DOWN the curve. Both are movements, not shifts. In your exam, examiners deduct marks if you call a movement a “shift” — the distinction matters.

A quick memory trick: if the word “price” appears in the explanation, it’s a movement. If any other word appears (costs, tax, subsidy, weather, technology), it’s a shift.

Why Supply Matters to Producers and Consumers

Understanding supply helps explain real-world price changes. When droughts cut cocoa yields in West Africa, chocolate manufacturers face higher input costs and lower raw-material availability — supply falls, and the price of chocolate rises. When a new semiconductor factory opens and chips become cheaper to make, the supply of smartphones and laptops increases, putting downward pressure on prices. Supply-side changes ripple through the entire market, affecting the price consumers pay and the profit producers earn.
exam_tip_html: The command word ‘Explain’ requires a chain of reasoning, not just a statement. If asked to explain why a fall in production costs increases supply, you must show the chain: costs fall → it becomes more profitable to produce → firms are willing to supply more at every price → the supply curve shifts to the right. A common mistake is to describe a movement along the supply curve when the question asks about a factor other than price — only a change in the price of the good itself causes a movement. Any other factor causes a shift. For ‘Analyse’ or ‘Evaluate’ questions, build a full cause-and-effect chain and, where asked to evaluate, consider how large the effect might be and whether other factors could limit it.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The law of supply states that, ceteris paribus, producers will supply more at higher prices and less at lower prices — giving the supply curve its upward slope.
  • A change in the price of the good causes a movement along the supply curve (extension or contraction); a change in any other factor — costs, technology, taxes, subsidies, weather, the number of firms, or productivity — shifts the entire curve left or right.
  • Supply shifts RIGHT (more supplied at every price) when costs fall, technology improves, a subsidy is given, or conditions are favourable; it shifts LEFT when costs rise, a tax is imposed, or adverse events (such as bad weather) restrict production.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the law of supply?
A. As price rises, quantity supplied falls, ceteris paribus.
B. As price rises, quantity supplied rises, ceteris paribus.
C. As price falls, quantity supplied rises, ceteris paribus.
D. Supply and price are unrelated.

A bakery currently supplies 800 loaves per week at a price of £2.00 each. The price rises to £2.50. The bakery increases supply to 1,000 loaves per week.

Calculate the percentage change in quantity supplied.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct method: percentage change = (new value − original value) ÷ original value × 100 = (1,000 − 800) ÷ 800 × 100; 1 mark for the correct answer of 25%.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a rise in the cost of raw materials is likely to reduce the supply of a good.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that higher raw material costs increase production costs; 1 mark for explaining that this reduces the profit margin at each price; 1 mark for concluding that firms will therefore be willing to supply less at every price, shifting the supply curve to the left.

practice_questions.text: A UK clothing manufacturer introduces new robotic machinery on its production line. Explain how this is likely to affect the supply of clothing in this market.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that new technology reduces the cost per unit of production; 1 mark for explaining that lower unit costs mean it is more profitable to produce at every price level; 1 mark for stating that the supply curve shifts to the right; 1 mark for applying this to the clothing market — for example, explaining that the manufacturer can now supply more jackets per week at the same price, increasing market supply and putting downward pressure on the price consumers pay.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a government subsidy given to electric vehicle (EV) manufacturers is likely to affect the supply of electric vehicles and the price consumers pay.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A full chain of reasoning — subsidy reduces production costs for EV manufacturers → lower costs mean greater profit at each price → firms willing to supply more at every price → supply curve shifts to the right → at the original price there is now excess supply → competition between producers puts downward pressure on price → equilibrium price falls and equilibrium quantity rises → consumers benefit from lower prices and greater choice. Analysis considers the size of the subsidy and whether all costs are affected.

Secure: Clear chain linking the subsidy to lower costs, rightward supply shift, and a fall in price, with some development of how equilibrium changes.

Developing: Identifies that a subsidy lowers costs and increases supply, but the link to price change is asserted rather than explained.

Emerging: States that a subsidy helps firms or lowers prices without developing the reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
"A rise in production costs is the most important factor that can reduce the supply of a good."

To what extent do you agree with this statement? Justify your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument that supports the statement (rises in wage costs, energy prices, or raw material costs raise per-unit costs, reduce profit margins, and shift supply left — a very direct and immediate transmission mechanism affecting all industries) AND challenges it with at least one alternative factor (e.g. bad weather is uncontrollable and can decimate agricultural supply entirely; a heavy new tax can shift supply left just as sharply; improved technology can offset cost rises and actually increase supply). Supported judgement: 'It depends on the industry — for manufacturing firms, costs are typically the dominant driver of supply changes, but for agricultural producers, weather can be equally or more powerful, being entirely outside the producer's control.' Uses the evaluation scaffold: size of change, time period, type of industry, and who is affected.

Secure: Both sides addressed with a supported judgement, though the judgement may rely on fewer dimensions.

Developing: One side developed well, the other briefly mentioned; judgement present but not fully supported.

Emerging: One-sided response with limited or no judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following would shift the supply curve to the RIGHT?
options: A rise in the price of the good
An increase in raw material costs

knowledge_checks.q: What does an 'extension of supply' mean?
options: The supply curve shifts to the right
The supply curve shifts to the left
Producers supply more because the price of the good has risen
Producers supply more because production costs have fallen

knowledge_checks.q: The law of supply states that as price rises, quantity supplied _____, ceteris paribus.
When a factor other than the price of the good changes — such as a fall in production costs — the entire supply curve _____.
Match each factor to its effect on supply:
right: Supply shifts left — less supplied at every price
Supply shifts right — more supplied at every price
Supply shifts right — lower unit costs
Supply shifts left — fewer goods available

flashcard_questions.q: What does the law of supply state?
flashcard_questions.a: As price rises, quantity supplied rises; as price falls, quantity supplied falls (ceteris paribus).

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the supply curve slope upward from left to right?
flashcard_questions.a: Higher prices give producers a greater incentive to produce and sell more.

flashcard_questions.q: What is an extension of supply?
flashcard_questions.a: A movement up the supply curve caused by a rise in the price of the good.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a contraction of supply?
flashcard_questions.a: A movement down the supply curve caused by a fall in the price of the good.

flashcard_questions.q: What causes a shift in the supply curve rather than a movement along it?
flashcard_questions.a: A change in any factor other than the price of the good itself.

flashcard_questions.q: Which direction does the supply curve shift when production costs rise?
flashcard_questions.a: To the left — less is supplied at every price.

flashcard_questions.q: Which direction does the supply curve shift when a government subsidy is given to producers?
flashcard_questions.a: To the right — lower costs mean more is supplied at every price.

flashcard_questions.q: How does improved technology affect supply?
flashcard_questions.a: It lowers unit costs, shifting the supply curve to the right.

flashcard_questions.q: A new tax is placed on a factory's carbon emissions. What happens to its supply curve?
flashcard_questions.a: It shifts to the left — higher costs reduce the quantity supplied at every price.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is agricultural supply particularly sensitive to weather?
flashcard_questions.a: Droughts, frosts or disease can destroy harvests, sharply reducing the quantity supplied.

flashcard_questions.q: What two conditions must producers meet for supply to exist — they must be willing and what else?
flashcard_questions.a: Able — producers must be both willing and able to sell at the given price.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'ceteris paribus' mean in the context of the law of supply?
flashcard_questions.a: All other factors are held constant — only the price of the good changes.

flashcard_questions.q: If the price of steel rises, what happens to the supply of cars?
flashcard_questions.a: Supply falls — higher input costs shift the supply curve to the left.

glossary_terms.definition: The quantity of a good or service that producers are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price over a given time period.
The principle that, ceteris paribus, producers will supply a greater quantity at a higher price and a smaller quantity at a lower price.
A change in the quantity supplied caused solely by a change in the price of the good, shown as movement along the existing curve.
A change in the quantity supplied at every price level caused by a factor other than the price of the good, shown as the entire curve moving left or right.
The expenses a firm incurs when producing goods or services, including raw materials, wages, energy and rent.
A levy placed on the production or sale of a good, which raises the producer's costs and shifts the supply curve to the left.
A payment from the government to a producer to lower their production costs, which shifts the supply curve to the right.
